samples.summary: New nesting cap is silently disabled on three write paths: `buildRowNode`/`buildCellNode` are called without the now-required `depth`, so `depth` becomes `undefined` → `NaN` and `depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH` is never true
samples.evidence: This delta changed the signatures to `buildCellNode(cell: TableCell, depth: number)` (line 417) and `buildRowNode(row: TableRow, depth: number)` (line 425), but three existing call sites were not updated: `insertTableRow` → `buildRowNode(row)` (line 2775), `insertTableColumn` → `buildCellNode(cells[r])` (line 2818), `updateTableCell` → `buildCellNode(cell)` (line 2858). These are TS2554 arity errors, and packages/frontend runs no `tsc` (package.json has only `vite build`, `eslint`, `vitest`), so they ship. At runtime the chain is: `buildCellNode(c, undefined)` → `buildBlockNode(b, undefined)` → `undefined >= 32` is false → `buildRowNode(row, undefined + 1)` = `NaN` → `NaN >= 32` is false and `NaN + 1` stays `NaN` forever. Every nested table written through a cell update, a row insert or a column insert is therefore written uncapped — the exact producer-side guard the diff's own comment says makes the readers/serializers safe ("Without the cap a model that never came out of this CRDT — a DOCX import, a paste — could write a chain deeper than every reader's stack"). `updateTableCell` is the workhorse path for cell content (including pasted cells holding nested tables), so the guard is bypassed on the most-used path while reading as covered. The only new test (`tests/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.test.ts:3650-3670`) exercises `setDocument`/`writeFullDocument`, so CI stays green.

samples.summary: Incremental block writes restart the depth counter at 0 regardless of how deep in the tree the node is inserted, so the nesting cap only binds on full-document writes
samples.evidence: `buildBlockNode(block)` is called with the default `depth = 0` at lines 1723 (replace block), 2312 and 2335 (insert block), 2371 (insert blocks), 2505 and 2584 — all of which can target a path inside an arbitrarily deep table cell (`resolveBlockTreePath` builds `[...tablePath, rowIdx, cellIdx, blockIdx]` recursively, line 1124). A table block inserted into a cell that already sits at depth 31 is serialized as if it were at depth 0, so up to 32 further levels are written into the CRDT past the cap. Nothing gates the gesture either: `Doc.insertTableInCell` (packages/docs/src/model/document.ts:885) and its caller `editor.ts:4237` perform no depth check, so a user (or a script driving the editor API) can nest tables one level at a time indefinitely. The resulting CRDT holds rows every reader truncates, and — because of the refusal added in this delta — every subsequent `writeFullDocument` on that document then throws. The cap is therefore enforced only on the one path (`writeFullDocument`) that also refuses outright, and not on the paths that actually grow nesting.

samples.summary: Snapshot normalizer's new depth cap counts only `row`-typed nodes, so a peer-written chain of any other node type still recurses without bound
samples.evidence: `normalizeYsonTreeNode` recurses into `node.children` for every node regardless of type, and only increments/stops on `node.type === 'row'` (lines 150-157). The Yorkie tree is written by peers with ordinary `tree.editByPath` calls and no schema is attached anywhere (no `schemaKey`/schema rule in packages/frontend/src; `client.attach` is called only with `initialRoot`), so a malicious collaborator can write e.g. a 20k-deep chain of `cell` (or any non-`row`) nodes. `unwrapYsonScalars` returns `Tree` by reference (unwrap-yson.ts:98) so it does not absorb the depth first — this walk is the first deep traversal, and it will overflow exactly as the doc comment says it would for the table-shaped case. Impact is bounded (the RangeError is catchable and `RevisionPreview` renders a role="alert"), but the guard advertises a class of protection it only partially provides; a total-recursion-depth cap rather than a row-typed one would close it.

samples.summary: The same untrusted-.docx walk that just gained a `<w:tbl>` nesting cap still recurses without bound over nested `<w:sdt>` content controls
samples.evidence: `blockChildElements` (line 649) unwraps `<w:sdt>`/`<w:sdtContent>` with `yield* DocxImporter.blockChildElements(content)` (line 656) and has no depth limit, while the comment added in this delta argues "A .docx is untrusted input — `<w:tbl>` nests inside `<w:tc>` with no format limit — so without the cap a crafted file overflows the stack right here, during import and before any layout runs" (line 251). `<w:sdt>` nests with no format limit either, and it is cheap: a few dozen bytes per level, highly compressible inside the zip. A crafted file therefore still overflows the stack in the importer, on the sibling recursion, defeating the stated goal of the new cap. Same for the paragraph/row/cell walks that all funnel through this generator (lines 326, 359, 427, 582, 762).

samples.summary: `PUT /content` accepts one nesting level more than the frontend reader materializes, so an API write can store exactly the document that makes the newly added `writeFullDocument` refusal throw for every editor client
samples.evidence: `assertValidBlock` rejects only when `depth > MAX_ELEMENT_DEPTH` (line 443, `MAX_ELEMENT_DEPTH = 32` at line 806) and recurses with `depth + 1` per cell level (line 491), so a body with tables at depths 0..32 — 33 nested levels — is accepted and written verbatim by `writeDocsRoot`, whose `buildBlockNode` (packages/backend/src/yorkie/docs-tree.ts:150) has no cap of its own. The frontend reader truncates any table at `depth >= 32`, and `hasTableAtNestingCap` (yorkie-doc-store.ts:446) then returns true for that model, so `writeFullDocument` (line 3260) throws for every client on that document. A holder of a write-scoped API key (or the CLI import flow) can therefore persist a document that makes the editor's `setDocument` path — e.g. applying a pending DOCX import over the open document, docs-view.tsx:396 — throw an unhandled Error for everyone, with no in-product way to repair it. The two caps should agree (`depth >= MAX_ELEMENT_DEPTH`, or the backend should share `MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH`).

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. `buildCellNode(cell: TableCell, depth: number)` (yorkie-doc-store.ts:417) and `buildRowNode(row: TableRow, depth: number)` (:425) take a non-optional `depth`, but three call sites pass none: `insertTableRow` at :2775, `insertTableColumn` at :2818, `updateTableCell` at :2858. At runtime `depth` is `undefined`, so the cap check `depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH` at :390 is false, and `buildRowNode(row, depth + 1)` at :392 makes it `NaN`, which stays `NaN` and never trips the cap at any depth — the nesting cap is fully disabled on those paths while the surrounding comment (:364-373) asserts it protects against a DOCX import or paste writing a chain "deeper than every reader's stack, i.e. a document nobody can open to repair." The arity error ships because packages/frontend/package.json:7-30 has no `tsc` script (only `vite build`, `eslint`, `vitest`), and vite strips types without checking. The paths are reachable from the UI (docs-table-context-menu.tsx:172,176,189,193) and `updateTableCell` is the general cell-content write path. This is a bypassed input-validation guard on attacker-influenced content (unsafe input handling / persistent availability), so it is in the security lane; peer read-side caps (crdt-tree.ts:225, snapshot-adapters.ts:152) mitigate but do not make the producer guard unreachable. No refutation ground applies.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. buildBlockNode (yorkie-doc-store.ts:378-392) only drops rows when its `depth` argument reaches MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH, and every incremental write calls it with the default depth 0: updateBlock:1723, insertBlock:2312, insertBlockAfter:2335, insertBlocksAfter:2371, and the split-block inserts at 2505 and 2584. None of them derives a depth from the target path, even though resolveBlockTreePath:1124-1160 (with recursive findBlockInTable:1106-1109) resolves arbitrarily deep [...tablePath,row,cell,block] targets inside nested cells. The cap is therefore enforced only inside writeFullDocument (yorkie-doc-store.ts:3260-3271 via hasTableAtNestingCap:446-457), the one path that refuses the write outright; and because getDocument() serves the incrementally patched cachedDoc (845-847, 2341-2343, 2385-2387) rather than a freshly truncated CRDT read, nesting can keep being extended past the cap, after which every subsequent full-document write (setHeader/setFooter/setDocument at 954/993/1039) throws. No guard elsewhere makes the deep-insert path unreachable, and a bypassable structural-input cap against peer/attacker-authored pathological CRDT shapes falls within unsafe-input-handling hardening for this lens, so I cannot refute it.

searchedFor: Grep computeSelectionRects call sites in editor.ts
finding.summary: Clamping bounds the rectangle to the table, but the table size is itself peer-chosen and `expandCellRangeForMerges` is an O(area) fixed-point scan run once per paint per peer selection
finding.evidence: `normalizeCellRange` clamps `start`/`end` to the table and then calls `expandCellRangeForMerges(ordered, table)` (line 146), a `while (changed)` loop whose inner `for (r) for (c)` scans the whole rectangle each pass. `normalizeRange` is reached from `computeSelectionRects`, which `editor.ts:2098` calls once per peer per paint (and `getSelectionRects` calls for the local selection). Row count is not banded anywhere — `MAX_TABLE_COLUMNS` (numeric-attrs.ts:95) caps columns at 256 but nothing caps `rows.length` — so a peer who writes a very large table and publishes `tableCellRange` `{start:{0,0}, end:{1e9,1e9}}` gets clamped to the *full table* and then re-scanned each frame, including on paint-only renders where the table layout is not recomputed. `maxCol` additionally reduces over every row on each call. Residual, not introduced: the change also newly routes *nested* tables into this expansion via the `resolveNestedTableLayout` fallback (line 191), widening what reaches it. A cheap fix is to cap the clamped rectangle's area (or the fixed-point pass count) rather than only its indices.

verdict.reason: The finding claims `expandCellRangeForMerges` is an uncapped `while (changed)` fixed-point scan whose only protection is index clamping in `normalizeCellRange`, and proposes capping the area or pass count as the fix. That cap already exists in the working tree. `packages/docs/src/view/selection.ts:40` defines `MAX_MERGE_EXPANSION_CELLS = 1 << 18`; line 114 seeds a shared `ScanBudget`; the loop at line 116 is `while (changed && budget.left > 0)` and both inner loops (lines 118-119) carry `&& budget.left > 0`, with `budget.left--` per visited cell at line 120. The `findMergeTopLeft` backtrack the reviewer cites as the superlinear term is charged to the same counter via `findMergeTopLeftBudgeted` (lines 67-92), which bails at line 79 when exhausted. Total work is therefore bounded at ~2^18 cell visits independent of the peer-chosen row count, so the peer-writes-a-huge-table-plus-`{1e9,1e9}`-range vector terminates promptly rather than re-scanning the full table each frame. A regression test for exactly that shape exists (test/view/cell-range-expand.test.ts:196-225, a 400x400 all-orphan-covered table asserted to return under 2s), and the nested-table fallback at line 242 feeds the same budgeted function, so it widens no unbounded path. Supporting details in the evidence are also off: the expansion call is at line 197 (not 146), and the `maxCol` reduce at lines 187-189 is O(rows), linear in the table and the same order as the layout that paints it. The residual bounded per-paint cost is not an exploitable availability break under the security rubric.

finding.summary: The cycle-guard sweep missed two recursive parent-map walks: `moveToNextCell` / `moveToPrevCell` recurse through `blockParentMap` with no visited set
finding.evidence: This PR adds `seen` guards to six walks over `blockParentMap` on the stated threat model that a peer can write two tables whose ids make the parent chain loop (ids come verbatim from CRDT attributes; the map is built in table-layout.ts:451 keyed on those ids, so duplicate ids across two tables produce A→B and B→A). Two walks over the same map were left unguarded: `moveToNextCell` recurses at text-editor.ts:6007 after moving the caret into the parent cell, and `moveToPrevCell` at text-editor.ts:6065 does the same. With a cyclic map, Tab / Shift+Tab at a table boundary ping-pongs between the two tables until the stack overflows (RangeError out of the key handler) — the same crash the PR closes in `Doc.findBlockInCells`. Confidence is low because the Tab path may pass `addRowAtEnd`, which takes the insert-row branch before the exit branch on the last cell; Shift+Tab (`moveToPrevCell`) has no such branch.

verdict.reason: The claimed unguarded recursion does not exist. Both walks carry the cycle guard: `moveToNextCell` is declared with a `seen?: Set<string>` parameter (text-editor.ts:5952) and guards its recursion at text-editor.ts:6013-6015 (`const visited = seen ?? new Set<string>(); if (visited.has(tableBlockId)) return false; visited.add(tableBlockId);`) immediately before recursing at text-editor.ts:6017. `moveToPrevCell` is identical: declared with `seen?: Set<string>` at text-editor.ts:6034 and guarded at text-editor.ts:6077-6079 before recursing at text-editor.ts:6081. The lines the finding cites as the recursion sites are something else entirely — 6007 is a non-recursive `cursor.moveTo` into the next sibling block, and 6065 is the `blockParentMap.get` lookup. Tracing a forged A→B→A parent cycle: the first exit records A in `visited`, the recursion records B, the third sees A already present and returns false, so the walk is bounded by the count of distinct table ids and no stack overflow is reachable from Tab or Shift+Tab. Only one file in packages/docs/src defines these methods, so there is no second unguarded copy. The doc comments at 5945-5950 and 6031-6032 also state that `seen` is the same cycle guard the other blockParentMap walks carry.
